items.title: Agentic Engineering Using Spec-Driven Development
items.text:
Abstract

This half-day workshop is designed to help development teams move beyond individual productivity gains to creating repeatable, institutional benefits with agentic coding tools. It emphasizes working effectively and responsibly by balancing human ownership and judgment with AI assistance to improve efficiency without sacrificing accountability. The workshop is structured around key phases of AI-driven engineering: requirements gathering, spec creation, implementation, and verification.

items.title: Workshop Flow
items.text:
1. Prerequisites: Clone the repo and run setup
  2. Presentation: Slides structured around key phases of AI-driven engineering: requirements gathering, spec creation, implementation, and verification
  3. Module 0 (Optional): Get to Know Your Agentic Tool
  4. Module 1: Requirements Gathering and Spec Creation
  5. Module 2: Implementation
  6. Module 3: Verification
  7. Module 4: Balancing Cost Through Efficiency — coming soon
  8. Module 5: Justifying an AI Workflow — coming soon

Info

This is a half-day workshop of five modules, plus an optional introductory module for those new to agentic tools. Modules 4 and 5 are being finalized and will be published here.

items.title: The Problem
items.text: Agentic coding tools unlock remarkable speed, but without a deliberate approach, that speed comes at the cost of human ownership. As developers offload more decisions to the agent, projects become harder to understand, maintain, and trust. The goal of Spec-Driven Development (SDD) is to reclaim that ownership intelligently: establishing clear points in the workflow where the human retains control, while still allowing the agent maximum autonomy everywhere else. SDD is not about slowing down; it's about maximizing agent autonomy without sacrificing project trust or human ownership.

items.title: Module 0 (Optional): Get to Know Your Agentic Tool
items.text: A hands-on introduction to agentic coding tools, covering core features like tool use, context, and permissioning. Participants practice prompt crafting, mode switching, and MCP server connections.

items.title: Module 1: Requirements Gathering and Spec Creation
items.text: Translate a vague product request into a spec the agent can build from. Participants use subagents to explore a brownfield codebase, define testable validation criteria, settle the open decisions themselves, and write a phased spec where every criterion traces to a phase.

items.title: Module 2: Implementation
items.text: Execute against the spec with the agent handling code changes autonomously. Participants set the autonomy boundary up front, supervise against the spec, and reset cleanly with git when a run derails.

items.title: Module 3: Verification
items.text: Take ownership back. Participants read the diff themselves, run the built-in review and an independent one, separate what needs a human decision from what doesn't, and make the ship/no-ship call.

items.text: Coming soon.

items.title: Module 0: Get to Know Your Agentic Tool
path: Module 0: Get to Know Your Agentic Tool

items.title: A Wordle Checker Script!
items.text:
wordle_check.py is a small program that scores a Wordle guess against a secret answer (🟩 green / 🟨 yellow / ⬜ gray). Copy and paste it into your IBM Bob editor.

You'll use this file to practice the mechanics of your agent: prompting, mode switching, built-in tools, and wiring up a simple GitHub MCP server.

wordle_check.py
"""
wordle_check.py — score a Wordle guess against the secret answer.

Given a 5-letter guess and the secret answer, return feedback for each
letter position:

    "green"  -> correct letter, correct position
    "yellow" -> letter is in the word, but a different position
    "gray"   -> letter is not in the word

Example:
    >>> score_guess("trace", "slate")
    ['yellow', 'gray', 'green', 'gray', 'green']
"""

WORD_LENGTH = 5

EMOJI = {"green": "\U0001F7E9", "yellow": "\U0001F7E8", "gray": "⬜"}


def score_guess(guess, answer):
    guess = guess.lower()
    answer = answer.lower()

    result = []
    for i in range(WORD_LENGTH):
        g = guess[i]
        if g == answer[i]:
            result.append("green")
        elif g in answer:
            result.append("yellow")
        else:
            result.append("gray")
    return result


def render(guess, answer):
    pattern = score_guess(guess, answer)
    squares = "".join(EMOJI[p] for p in pattern)
    return f"{guess.upper()}  {squares}"


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # A few sample rounds. The answer is SLATE.
    print(render("trace", "slate"))
    print(render("crane", "slate"))
    print(render("eerie", "slate"))
path: Module 0: Get to Know Your Agentic Tool

items.title: 1. Two Kinds of Prompts
items.text:
Ask your agent about the file twice:

  • Lazy: "Does this look correct?"
  • Structured: "Walk through score_guess and check how it handles a guess that repeats a letter the answer only contains once. Give a concrete example."

Notice how differently the two prompts land. Which one surfaces a real problem?

Note

Both prompts should surface the bug, but the structured prompt will give you a far more useful response. The takeaway isn't specific to this file: the more precisely you define what you want the agent to check, the more useful its output will be.
path: Module 0: Get to Know Your Agentic Tool

items.title: 2. Test Out the Modes
items.text:
Bob 2.0 ships with 3 streamlined modes (Ask, Plan, Agent). Move through them in order and notice how the agent's behavior and available tools change at each step:

  • Ask: Map out the file. Have it explain the logic trace and pin down the bug.
  • Plan: Lock the implementation plan. Have it propose a fix (don't let it edit yet).
  • Agent: Implement. Have it apply the fix.
path: Module 0: Get to Know Your Agentic Tool

items.title: 3. Use the Built-in Tools (read + write + run)
items.text: Now prove the fix holds. Ask your agent to write a few test cases to a new file (including a guess with a repeated letter, e.g. guess EERIE, answer SLATE) and run it. Does the output match what real Wordle would show? Paste back the original version to watch the same test fail; that's the bug you just fixed.
path: Module 0: Get to Know Your Agentic Tool

items.title: 4. Use the GitHub MCP Server (Optional)
items.text:
Setting up the GitHub MCP server for GitHub Enterprise

1. In Bob, go to Settings → MCP, search for GitHub, and click Install. Select your workspace as the installation scope.

2. Generate a PAT at github.ibm.com/settings/tokens/new with at minimum repo scope (or just check all).

3. Set the following:

  • PAT: paste your token from step 2
  • Hostname: https://github.ibm.com
  • Toolsets: repos,issues,pull_requests

4. Open .bob/mcp.json and change "command": "docker" to "command": "podman".

5. Verify the connection (optional)

Run this to confirm the server starts and your PAT is valid: 

echo '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2024-11-05","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"test","version":"0"}}}' | \
  podman run -i --rm \
    -e GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN=<token> \
    -e GITHUB_HOST=https://github.ibm.com \
    ghcr.io/github/github-mcp-server 2>&1 | head -4
You should see both: 
token scopes fetched for filtering   ← auth worked, PAT is valid
GitHub MCP Server running on stdio   ← server started cleanly
Any error on either line tells you exactly what's wrong (bad host format, bad token, network issue) without needing to debug a silent disconnect in Bob.

Your file lives on your machine, but the GitHub MCP can still reach out to GitHub for you:

  • Fetch the reference: pull the README from hbattu/wordle_kata via the GitHub MCP and confirm the correct rule for repeated letters. Compare it to what your agent found in step 1.

  • Stretch goal (if your GitHub token allows): fork hbattu/wordle_kata via the MCP and either file an issue describing the bug or open a PR with your fix. This is a reflection of the real open-source flow, driven entirely through the agent.
path: Module 0: Get to Know Your Agentic Tool

items.title: Module 1: Requirements Gathering and Spec Creation
path: Module 1: Requirements Gathering and Spec Creation

items.title: The Codebase
items.text:
Finch Financial is an internal operations console for a fictional neobank. The app is already running with the following functionality built:

  • Sign in via email and password (all users share the password Password123!)
  • Browse and filter customer accounts by status and name
  • Search and filter transactions across all accounts
  • View an account's detail page with transactions, memos, and audit log
  • RBAC: analysts see active and frozen accounts; supervisors can also see closed accounts. Only supervisors can add memos.
path: Module 1: Requirements Gathering and Spec Creation

items.title: Your Task
items.text:
Pick one of the two product requests:

1. Freeze and unfreeze customer accounts when suspicious activity is detected.

An ops analyst notices Northgate Properties just sent a $280,000 wire to Cayman Holdings Ltd, with no prior history of transfers anywhere near that size. They can't freeze the account themselves (that requires a supervisor), so they flag it to their supervisor, who logs in and freezes the account with a reason.

2. Flag suspicious transactions for follow-up review, with a supervisor resolution workflow.

An analyst notices Tran Consulting Group has a series of rapid international wires in both directions. They flag a transaction with a reason. The flag appears in a queue. A supervisor reviews it and resolves it.

See product-requests.md for further details.

This module takes a product request to a spec in one session. You own every decision in it; the agent explores, drafts, and asks. It runs in two halves: understand the ground your feature lands on, then decide and write.

Stay in Ask mode while you explore (the agent can read the repo but not change it). Switch to Plan mode when it's time to write (it can edit files but not execute anything).
path: Module 1: Requirements Gathering and Spec Creation

items.title: Part A: Understand
path: Module 1: Requirements Gathering and Spec Creation

items.title: 1. Map the Territory with Subagents
items.text:
Exploring a codebase is wide and noisy. Don't do it in your main conversation. Hand each question to a subagent: it reads in its own context window and returns only a summary, so the reading never piles up in yours. Ask for the files, in order, and nothing else.

"I'm adding [your request] and I'm new to this codebase. Use subagents to find: the most similar existing feature, traced from API call to database and tests; the rules the code enforces when the relevant data changes; and the parts of the app this feature would touch. Summaries only. Don't plan or write code yet."

Keep it scoped. Map only the slice your feature actually touches, and avoid ingesting the whole repo.
path: Module 1: Requirements Gathering and Spec Creation

items.title: 2. Define Your Validation Criteria (Most Important)
items.text:
Requirements aren't only about behavior; they're about how you'll prove the behavior is right. Ask what the repo already gives you to verify against (the type system, the test setup, RBAC rules, audit-log guarantees). Then turn each expected outcome from the product request into a criterion with a pass condition, one per outcome.

"What does this repo already give me to verify a change against? Then turn the expected outcomes into validation criteria, one per outcome, each with a pass condition."

This is what Module 3 verifies against, so "it should work" won't cut it.
path: Module 1: Requirements Gathering and Spec Creation

items.title: 3. Surface the Open Questions
items.text:
Ask what the code can't settle: business rules, edge cases, desired behavior. Those are your decisions, not the agent's. Capture them as questions. You'll settle them in Part B.

"What open questions require my input that you can't settle from the code alone?"
path: Module 1: Requirements Gathering and Spec Creation

items.title: 4. Spot-check the Agent
items.text: Don't take the agent's word for it. Open one or two files it cited and confirm its claims yourself. Note where the agent was right, vague, or wrong.
path: Module 1: Requirements Gathering and Spec Creation

items.title: Part B: Decide and Write
items.text: Switch to Plan mode.
path: Module 1: Requirements Gathering and Spec Creation

items.title: 5. Write requirements.md
items.text: Have the agent write the requirements from the conversation: the task, the validation criteria, the relevant files, and the open questions. Requirements only: no plan, no code. If it starts planning, stop it.
path: Module 1: Requirements Gathering and Spec Creation

items.title: 6. Settle the Open Questions
items.text:
Have the agent interview you: one question at a time, with a proposed default for each. The repo ships an interview skill that does exactly this and records every decision in the file.

"Interview me about the open questions in @requirements.md."

Accept or override each default. When it shows the assumptions it's making, confirm them or correct them. Being on the answering end is what surfaces assumptions you didn't know you were making. This is where ownership is won or lost: rubber-stamp the defaults and you've handed the agent your design.
path: Module 1: Requirements Gathering and Spec Creation

items.title: 7. Draft spec.md
items.text:
Now ask for the plan. Phases in dependency order; each phase names the criteria it satisfies and how to check them; every validation criterion traces to a phase. Reject non-steps like "implement X": each phase should say what changes, where, and how you'll know it worked on its own.

"Using @requirements.md, draft a spec.md: phases in dependency order, each naming the criteria it satisfies and how to check them. Every criterion must trace to a phase. No vague steps."

Tip

Stop at a minimum viable spec: one where you understand and accept the architectural decisions and their level of detail. Don't over-invest chasing perfect.
path: Module 1: Requirements Gathering and Spec Creation

items.title: 8. Audit it (optional)
items.text:
If time allows, have a fresh subagent check the spec against the requirements: every criterion in a phase, no vague steps, nothing the requirements didn't ask for. A reviewer that didn't write the draft catches what the drafter can't.

Tip

requirements.md and spec.md are the only things that cross into Module 2. The conversation doesn't. If the spec is clear enough that someone else could implement from it, you're ready.

Security note

Don't paste secrets into prompts or have the agent open .env.
path: Module 1: Requirements Gathering and Spec Creation

items.title: Module 2: Implementation
items.text:
Start a new session, then point your agent at the spec.md you created in Module 1. You'll work in Agent mode.

The fresh context is deliberate. The spec is the handoff, and a cold start is what forces it to carry the work on its own. If the session still remembers your Module 1 interview, a spec with gaps in it will still produce good code, and you'll never find out.

Auto-Acceptance

This is the highest-autonomy phase: the spec does the thinking, the agent does the work. Decide up front what the agent may run without asking (reads, edits, the test and typecheck commands) and what still needs your approval. Do this work first, so you can then get out of the way and let the agent make progress.

items.title: 1. Set Your Guardrails Up Front
items.text: Decide before you start what the agent can run on its own and what needs your approval. Auto-approve the safe, reversible things: reads, edits, and the project's checks. Gate anything risky or irreversible. Doing this up front is what lets you step back afterward.

items.title: 2. Hand it the Spec and Let it Run
items.text:
Point the agent at spec.md and let it implement with minimal intervention. Resist the urge to do it yourself: the point is to see a good spec carry the work.

"Implement @spec.md phase by phase. Run each phase's checks and report before moving to the next."

items.title: 3. Supervise Against the Spec
items.text:
Expect it to run straight through rather than stopping between phases. It will report each phase and keep going. Use its progress tracking to keep a view and spot-check as you go: don't hover over every token (that defeats the purpose), but don't wave through large or risky changes either.

If it drifts from the spec, correct it against the spec. Don't negotiate.

"Phase N was supposed to X. It did Y. Fix it to match the spec. Don't change the spec."

items.title: 4. If it Derails, Reset
items.text:
Editing the spec while the agent is working will usually throw it off. If it's going off the rails, or the spec turns out too weak, stop, fix the spec, and restart cleanly:

git restore .

Then run the implementation prompt again. That command reverts every tracked file the agent touched and leaves your requirements.md and spec.md alone, because they're untracked. A module of work can't be destroyed by the undo.

Never git clean

That deletes untracked files, which is exactly where your requirements.md and spec.md live.

Tip

Little hands-on ownership here means more to verify next. Let the agent move fast, and plan to verify carefully in Module 3.

items.title: Module 3: Verification
items.text: Setup: Work from the change you built in Module 2. This is where ownership and trust climb back up: the agent generated the code, now you take responsibility for it. The agent helps you review; the judgment is yours.

items.title: 1. See the Blast Radius
items.text:
git diff --stat main

One screen: every file the implementation touched and how much. Read it before anything else.

items.title: 2. Review it Yourself First
items.text:
Open one file and read it as the author, not a spectator. This is how you take ownership back from the agent. Watch for the classic AI code smells:

  • Dead code, hardcoded values, and half-finished abstractions
  • Missed edge cases and outdated library usage
  • "Lazy" shortcuts: less code instead of correct code
  • Locally correct but globally wrong: right in the file, wrong for the system

Sort what you find: structural gaps go back to the spec, content errors you fix, loose code you tighten.

items.title: 3. Run the Built-in Review
items.text:
Run /review, compare against main, include uncommitted changes, and start it. Read the findings.

Don't click "Fix with Bob." A fix the agent applies to its own work is a decision you didn't make. Fixes go through the spec (step 6), not through a button.

items.title: 4. Run an Independent Review
items.text:
Start a new session in Ask mode and have it review the diff against your spec and requirements: does the code match the spec, is it safe for a regulated fintech app, and would the tests actually fail if a requirement were broken?

"Review the diff against @spec.md and @requirements.md: does the code match the spec, is it safe for a regulated fintech app, and would the tests fail if a requirement were broken? Skip what matches. Report what matters and mark which findings need a human decision."

Why a new session

The agent that wrote this code shares its own blind spots. Review it in the same window and you get the same assumptions on both ends: code that appears correct, passes its own review, and is still missing something. A fresh session reviews the diff, not the memory of writing it. Even so, notice what it doesn't raise: a diff review sees what's there, never what was never written.

items.title: 5. The Human Gate
items.text:
Three questions, answered by you, not the agent:

  1. What did /review find that the independent review didn't, and the reverse?
  2. Of the findings marked as needing a human decision, which would block shipping at your organization?
  3. Would this ship, and who signs?

Judge by blast radius (how much it can break) and use-case sensitivity (how much it matters if it does).

items.title: 6. Close the Loop (optional)
items.text:
If a finding is real, the fix belongs in the spec, not in a patch. Add the agreed change to the relevant phase of spec.md, switch to Agent mode, and re-implement that phase only.

"Phase N of @spec.md changed. Re-implement that phase and run its checks."

This is the whole discipline in one move: the spec stays the source of truth, and the code follows it.

Tip

AI fits into your existing review and governance process; it doesn't replace it. If you have a neighbor, swap diffs and review each other's change: a human reviewing AI code they didn't commission is exactly what breaks the loop. End this module with code you'd put your name on.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
Complete these steps before the workshop to make sure your environment is ready.

The app runs on SQLite — an embedded database file, with no server and no containers. Setup is two commands.

items.title: 1. Install Tools
items.text:
macOS only — Install Homebrew (if you don't have it)

Step 1 — Check if Homebrew is already installed: 

brew --version
✅ If you see a version number (e.g. Homebrew 4.4.0) — you're done, skip this section.

❌ If you get command not found — continue below.

Step 2 — Install Xcode command line tools: 

xcode-select --install

Step 3 — Install Homebrew: 

/bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)"

Step 4 — Set up Homebrew in your shell: 

echo 'eval "$(/opt/homebrew/bin/brew shellenv)"' >> ~/.zprofile
eval "$(/opt/homebrew/bin/brew shellenv)"

Step 5 — Verify: 

brew --version
# Homebrew 4.4.0

items.title: Node.js 22+
items.text:
Node 22 or newer is required

The database driver ships prebuilt binaries for Node 22+. On older versions npm install will fail trying to compile it from source.

macOSLinux (Ubuntu/Debian)Windows 
brew install node@22
node --version

curl -fsSL https://deb.nodesource.com/setup_22.x | sudo -E bash -
sudo apt-get install -y nodejs
node --version

Download and install from nodejs.org

items.title: Git
items.text:
macOSLinux (Ubuntu/Debian)Windows 
brew install git

sudo apt-get install git

Download and install from git-scm.com

items.title: 2. Clone and Set Up
items.text:
git clone https://github.com/hbattu73/finch-financial.git
cd finch-financial
npm run setup

npm run setup installs dependencies, creates api/.env with working defaults, creates the SQLite database, and seeds it with workshop data. No configuration is needed.

items.title: 3. Start the App
items.text:
npm run dev

This starts the API (port 3000) and the web app (port 5173) together, with their output colour-coded in one terminal. Stop both with Ctrl+C.

Open http://localhost:5173 and log in with any of the workshop credentials. All users share the password Password123!.

items.title: Verify It Works
items.text:
You should see:

  • A list of customer accounts with status badges
  • The ability to filter by account status and name
  • An account detail page with transactions, memos, and audit log

If you can browse accounts and view transactions, you're ready.

Reset data at any time

The seed script is idempotent. To restore the original workshop data at any point, run: 

npm run seed
To start completely fresh, delete the database file and re-run setup: 
rm api/finch.db
npm run setup

items.title: Next Steps
items.text: Proceed to the Presentation to get started.

items.title: Testing
items.text:
Both suites are standalone — no running server and no database setup. Backend tests run the Express app in-process with supertest against a fresh in-memory SQLite database per test file. Frontend tests mock fetch.

Your development data is never touched by a test run.

# Everything
npm test

# One workspace
npm test -w api
npm test -w web

# A specific file, or watch mode
npm test -w api -- accounts.test.ts
npm test -w api -- --watch

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text:
npm install fails building better-sqlite3

Almost always an out-of-date Node. Check your version: 

node --version
If it's below 22, install Node 22+ (see above) and re-run: 
npm run setup

Port 3000 or 5173 is already in use

Another process is holding the port. Find and stop it:

macOS / LinuxWindows 
lsof -ti:3000 | xargs kill
lsof -ti:5173 | xargs kill

netstat -ano | findstr :3000
taskkill /PID <pid> /F

Alternatively, set a different API port in api/.env.

npm run dev says dependencies are not installed

Run the setup command first: 

npm run setup

Clone fails with an authentication error

If you see: 

remote: Password authentication is not available for Git operations.
remote: You must use a personal access token or SSH key.
Authenticate using one of the following:

  • SSH key (recommended) — Generate an SSH key and add it to your GitHub account
  • Personal access token — Create a personal access token and use it in place of your password when prompted
